title: When practice fails you
hookLine: practice isn't a cure-all; get help when you need it
tomorrow: why would a text praise the one who fell?

cards: Some nights the breathing that used to settle everything just doesn't.
Mai's text came in the middle of the night: finals, early shifts, barely any sleep for days, and when she sits, her heart races louder instead of quieter. Practice was supposed to fix this.

An old story looks at that moment from the other side. In the Vinaya, the Buddha is walking through the monks' lodgings with Ananda when they find a monk lying sick in his own mess, too weak to get up.
Nobody has come to help him.

teach.h: THE BUDDHA WASHES THE SICK MONK.
teach.b: The Buddha asks him why no one tends him. Because I'm no use to the other monks, he says. So the Buddha and Ananda fetch water, wash him, and lift him onto a bed.
Then the Buddha calls the monks together. You have no mother and no father here to look after you, he tells them.

teach.h: IF YOU DON'T TEND ONE ANOTHER, WHO WILL?
teach.b: If you don't tend one another, who will? Whoever would tend me should tend the sick. That's the teaching: in Buddhism, caring for the sick isn't a break from the path; the Buddha puts it at the center.
And getting care isn't failing at practice.
The Vinaya has a whole section on the medicines monks may take. It even tells of Jivaka, a physician, treating the Buddha himself, with medicine given through lotus flowers to smell.

Meditation was never meant to replace a doctor, a counselor, or a parent who notices. Mai told her mom, Linh, a pharmacist, and they made an appointment. It won't all be fixed by next week, and that's all right.
If you're ever in danger, or thinking about hurting yourself, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.

how: Buddhist monasteries care for sick monks as the Vinaya directs, and monks may take medicine; teachers commonly encourage students to see a doctor or counselor alongside their practice when they're struggling.

games.q: what does “when practice fails you” mean?
o: times when practice alone can't carry what you face
giving up meditation for good after a setback
a sign that you've chosen the wrong teacher

games.q: the sick monk — tap the pairs.
p: said he was no use to the others
washed him and lifted him to a bed
a physician who treated the Buddha
as you would tend the Buddha

s: if you meditate well enough, you won't need a doctor
the Vinaya lists medicines for monks, and the physician Jivaka treated the Buddha himself.
the Buddha washed a sick monk with his own hands
he and Ananda washed him and lifted him onto a bed.
in the story, the monks left him alone because the Buddha told them to rest
the monk said it was because he was no use to them. the Buddha corrected the monks.

games.q: your friend has felt panicky for weeks and hopes more meditation will fix it on its own. what fits today's story?
o: more meditation; if it isn't working, she's doing it wrong.
keep practicing, and also talk to a doctor or someone she trusts.
quit meditating; it obviously doesn't help her.
games.why: the Buddha took medicine and told the monks to tend the sick. practice and care belong together.

practice: Bring to mind one person you could actually tell if things got hard: a parent, a friend, a doctor, a teacher. Picture their face and the one sentence you'd say. If someone comes to mind who might need that from you, hold them too.
Nothing to send; just know the door is there.

wordCard.voice: When practice fails you: the times meditation can't carry it alone. The Buddha took medicine, and told his monks to tend the sick.

orig.note: Pali: sick, ill. Tending the sick is what the Buddha asked of his monks: whoever would tend me should tend the sick.

carryVoice: Get help too: whoever would tend the Buddha, he said, should tend the sick. Take good care.

sources.ref: Vinaya Pitaka, Mahavagga VIII.26 (the monk sick with dysentery; 'whoever would tend me should tend the sick')
Vinaya Pitaka, Mahavagga VIII.1 (Jivaka treats the Buddha with medicated lotuses)
